sentences.text: She asked her grandmother in the last week of March, in the kitchen at Ballyroe, sitting down, having planned the question for three days and then abandoning the plan entirely and just asking it.
Why did he wear a watch that didn't work.
Her grandmother put the tea down.

She said that it had stopped on the eleventh of June 2011, which was a Saturday, and that they had both been in the car outside the hospital in Galway at the time, and that they had been in that car park for a very long while that afternoon and had not gone in, and that the watch had stopped somewhere in that.

She said that he had taken it to be fixed twice and had brought it back both times unfixed, and that on the second occasion the man in Galway had told him it would cost twenty euro and forty minutes, and that he had said no thank you and had walked out.

She said that Orla should not make it into more than it was, because he had never once explained himself about it, and that she had asked him exactly twice in fourteen years and had been told, both times, that he was fond of it.
Then she said: "But he checked it.
That's the thing I'd say if you're wanting a thing to hold.
He'd look at it.

Two, three times in a day, all those years, he'd turn his wrist over and look at a watch that said twenty past four, and then he'd get on with what he was at." Orla went back to the wood on the second of April.
She sat down on the floor of the chamber and she said it out loud, all of it, the whole thing, taking about four minutes and getting it in the wrong order and having to go back twice.
The badger listened, the way it always listened.

Then it went to the third row near the left-hand passage and took the watch out of the wall and put it on the floor between them, and went back down one of the passages she was never allowed down, and Orla sat there on her own for a while and then went home.
She is thirty-four.
The watch says twenty past four.
She has never had it fixed and has been asked about it perhaps a hundred times, and what she says is that she is fond of it.

She has been back to the beech on the boundary bank six or seven times as an adult, and the hole is there, and she has never once put her arm down it, and she thinks about the hundred and five other things in that wall more often than she expected to.
Because that is the part that got her, in the end, and it took her until her twenties to see it properly.
The catalogue is complete.
Every single thing in that wall has an entry, and every entry says what the thing was doing, and the badger has kept all of it dry since 1911.
And almost nobody is ever going to come and say it.
